---
title: "Building your own skills"
subtitle: "Package a workflow once, invoke it by name forever — with three of my own as worked examples."
---

Contrary to the impression you might get online, I don't use many skills.
The three below are simply the tasks I found myself doing over and over, the
same way each time — so I wrote them down. That's the whole reason to build a
skill: not novelty, but repetition. If you're not repeating something, you
don't need one.

A **skill** is a reusable instruction set you can invoke by name. Instead of
re-typing the same multi-step prompt every time ("scaffold a Pluto notebook
with sliders, estimation, and identification diagnostics…"), you write it
down once as a `SKILL.md` file and call it with `/your-skill`.

Mechanically, a skill is just a folder with a `SKILL.md` inside it:

```
my-skill/
└── SKILL.md
```

The file has a short YAML header (the "frontmatter") and a body. The body
is the prompt Claude runs when you invoke the skill; the header tells Claude
what the skill is for and how it's allowed to run.

I keep mine in a small public repo, [myccskills](https://github.com/moshialam/myccskills),
with three skills in it. They're worth walking through because they show two
different shapes a useful skill can take.

## The three skills

### `/plutonb` — a knowledge skill

**What it does:** scaffolds a [Pluto.jl](https://plutojl.org/) notebook for a
structural-econometrics simulation — model primitives as a `struct`, a data
generating process with explicit seeds, MLE/GMM estimation with a
true-vs-estimated comparison table, interactive `@bind` sliders,
identification diagnostics, and a LaTeX appendix. You call it with a model
description: `/plutonb a Roy model of occupational choice`.

**How it's built:** it's essentially my "how I want a structural notebook
built" knowledge, written down. The body is a long, structured set of
instructions — cell order, parameter-transformation conventions (`exp()` for
variances, `tanh()` for correlations), how to document exclusion
restrictions, a quality checklist. The frontmatter passes the model
description in via `$ARGUMENTS`:

```yaml
---
name: plutonb
description: Create a Pluto.jl notebook for structural econometrics
  simulations. Use when the user asks to create a Pluto notebook,
  simulation notebook, or structural model notebook.
user-invocable: true
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep
argument-hint: "[model-name-or-description]"
---
```

This is the most common kind of skill to write first: take a task you do
repeatedly and do *a particular way*, and encode that way once.

### `/evolution` — a context-gathering skill

**What it does:** reads a project's git history and tells the story of how it
evolved — phases, milestones, pivots, and what's being worked on now. Run it
in any repo with `/evolution`, or scope it (`/evolution 20`,
`/evolution 2025-01`).

**How it's built:** this one demonstrates two features beyond a plain prompt.
First, it **pre-loads context by running shell commands** with the `` ! ``
prefix — the output is injected into the prompt before Claude starts:

```markdown
### Full git log with file-level changes
!`git log --stat --all --date=short --format="%h %ad %s" | head -500`
```

Second, the frontmatter runs it in a separate, read-only sub-agent so it
doesn't clutter your main session:

```yaml
context: fork
agent: Explore
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Glob, Grep
```

The body is then just instructions for turning that git history into a
readable narrative.

### `/remind` — also context-gathering

**What it does:** a snapshot of where a project stands when you come back to
it after time away — branch and remote status, uncommitted work, recent
commits, structure, and any saved context from `CLAUDE.md` / `MEMORY.md`.

**How it's built:** same shape as `/evolution` — `!`-prefixed commands
pre-load `git status`, the branch list, recent commits, and the directory
listing, then a forked `Explore` agent reads `CLAUDE.md` and `MEMORY.md` and
summarizes. It's a good template to copy when you want a "gather some state,
then summarize it" skill.

## The building blocks, in one place

Everything above is assembled from a small set of pieces:

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| `SKILL.md` in a named folder | The skill itself; the folder name is the default skill name |
| `name`, `description` | The `description` is what Claude matches on to decide the skill applies — write it carefully |
| `user-invocable: true` | Lets you call it explicitly with `/name` |
| `allowed-tools:` | Restricts which tools the skill may use |
| `argument-hint:` | Documents what to pass after the name |
| `$ARGUMENTS` (in the body) | Where your input gets substituted |
| `` !`command` `` (in the body) | Runs a shell command and injects its output before Claude starts |
| `context: fork` + `agent: Explore` | Runs the skill in a separate read-only sub-agent |

The two shapes worth knowing: **knowledge skills** (`/plutonb`) that encode
"the way I do X," and **context skills** (`/evolution`, `/remind`) that
gather state with `` ! `` commands and then reason over it.

## Installing them

Claude Code reads personal skills from `~/.claude/skills/`. There are two
ways to get mine onto your machine.

**Option A — copy the skills you want.** Simplest, and it won't disturb any
skills you already have:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moshialam/myccskills.git
cp -R myccskills/plutonb ~/.claude/skills/      # repeat for evolution, remind
```

**Option B — symlink the whole repo.** This is how I run them, so my edits
stay under version control. Only do this if `~/.claude/skills` isn't already
holding skills of your own, since it points the entire directory at the repo:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moshialam/myccskills.git
ln -sfn "$(pwd)/myccskills" ~/.claude/skills
```

Either way, verify with `ls ~/.claude/skills` and then, inside Claude Code,
type `/` to confirm `plutonb`, `evolution`, and `remind` show up.

::: {.callout-note}
To scope a skill to a single project instead of your whole machine, put it
in `.claude/skills/` inside that project's folder rather than in
`~/.claude/skills/`. Project skills are a good way to share a skill with
coauthors through the project's own git repo.
:::

## Writing your own

The fastest way to start is to copy one of these as a template and edit it:

- Repetitive task you do a specific way → copy `plutonb`, replace the body
  with your instructions, update `name`/`description`/`argument-hint`.
- "Gather some state, then summarize" → copy `remind`, swap the `` ! ``
  commands for whatever you want pre-loaded.

Good candidates from elsewhere on this site: a `/audit-replication` skill
built from the [replication-package walkthrough](../examples/replication-package.qmd),
or a `/reorganize-project` skill from the
[messy-project walkthrough](../getting-started/reorganize-a-messy-project.qmd).
Once you've done either of those by hand twice, it's worth writing down.

See also [Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills](memory-and-claude-md.qmd) for how skills
sit alongside the other ways of giving Claude persistent context.
